October brought 165,000 new jobs, far above the 59,000 economists expected, while inflation ran at 3.7% in September. Before this morning's report, traders saw about a 70% chance the Fed raises rates again in December, after its first hike since 2023 in September. This video explains why the Fed hikes, what the 1980 and 2022 hiking cycles did, and what another hike would mean for your credit card, mortgage, savings, 401(k) and job.

0:43 What happened this week
2:17 Why the Fed hikes
3:34 A short history of hikes
4:59 Your loans and savings
6:50 Your 401(k) and your job

Sources: Bureau of Labor Statistics (October jobs report, Nov 6, 2026; September CPI, Oct 14, 2026) via CNBC, Bloomberg and Yahoo Finance; Federal Reserve decisions (Sept 16 and Oct 28, 2026; Dec 10, 2025); CME FedWatch via CNBC and ABC News (Nov 5-6, 2026); Freddie Mac PMMS (Nov 5, 2026); Bankrate (Nov 4, 2026); CNN and Kiplinger (Nov 5, 2026); Federal Reserve History (Volcker era).

News and education, not financial advice.
